title: CELPIP Reading Practice Test 16
instructions: Read each passage carefully and answer the questions. You may scroll back within each part.

emails.subject: Stepping back from Thursday shifts
emails.body:
Dear Priya,

After four years I am stepping back from the Thursday distribution shift, effective at the end of June. I want to explain why, because I think it is fixable for the next person and I would rather be useful than simply absent.

It is not the work and it is not the people. Both have been the best part of my week.

It is that my four-hour shift has become a six-hour shift without anyone deciding it should. The van now arrives at 1:30 rather than noon, so unloading runs into distribution; the second afternoon volunteer post has been unfilled since February; and the closing paperwork was moved to us in March. Each of those was reasonable on its own. Together they added two hours to a shift I agreed to as four, and nobody ever asked me whether that was all right, because nobody was tracking the total.

I am not upset and I am not asking for anything. I am 71 and six hours on my feet is simply beyond what I can sustain. If the shift were four hours again I would stay.

With warm regards,
Marguerite Delacroix

emails.subject: RE: Stepping back from Thursday shifts
emails.body:
Dear Marguerite,

You have written the most useful letter I have received in this job, and I am sorry it took you leaving to produce it.

You are right that nobody decided. I made all three of those changes and I did not add them up, because each one crossed my desk separately and each looked small. That is not an explanation that helps you; it is just what happened, and it is exactly the failure your letter describes.

I have checked the roster this morning. Two other Thursday volunteers are in the same position and neither has said anything, which I suspect means the same thing it meant with you until you wrote.

What changes from next week. The shift returns to four hours: the van slot is moving back to noon, which I can do because the depot offered it in March and I did not take it. Closing paperwork moves to the evening stock team. And I am posting the afternoon vacancy properly rather than hoping someone notices it.

One thing I will not do is ask you to reconsider. You said if the shift were four hours you would stay, and I would rather fix it and let you decide than fix it and immediately make that your decision to justify. The Thursday shift is yours whenever you want it, in June or in a year, and I will not ask again.

With thanks and some embarrassment,
Priya

passages.title: What Actually Makes People Keep Volunteering
passages.content:
Recruitment campaigns for volunteers are built on motivation — the desire to help, to belong, to give something back. Those motives are real and they explain why people start. They explain very little about why people stop, and retention rather than recruitment is where most organisations lose capacity.

Surveys of departing volunteers rarely produce the reason campaigns assume. People seldom say they stopped caring. They describe a role that grew, a commitment that outran what they agreed to, or an organisation that never noticed either. Scope creep is the most commonly reported cause of departure and the least often addressed, partly because it accumulates through small reasonable decisions that no single person experiences as a decision at all.

Recognition is where organisations most often act and most often misjudge. The evidence suggests volunteers value being asked before their role changes far more than they value being thanked after it does not. An annual appreciation event alongside a role that has quietly doubled reads as an organisation that is watching the wrong thing. Small, specific and timely acknowledgement outperforms ceremony, and costs less.

The demographics carry a warning that is easy to miss. Volunteering hours are heavily concentrated in a small proportion of volunteers, and that group is older on average than the volunteer base as a whole. Organisations frequently describe having hundreds of volunteers while depending on a few dozen, and the dependency is invisible until one of them leaves. The risk is not that volunteering is declining in general; it is that a specific irreplaceable group is ageing while the metrics report a healthy total.

Barriers to starting are also less about willingness than organisations assume. Unclear time commitments, slow onboarding and long background-check waits lose more prospective volunteers than a shortage of interest does. Someone who offers time and hears nothing for a month has usually filled that time with something else, and the organisation records it as a person who changed their mind.

The practical conclusion is unglamorous. Retention is mostly an administrative discipline rather than a motivational one: define the role, track whether it is still the role, ask before changing it, and answer people quickly when they volunteer.

passages.title: Should Long-Term Volunteers Receive a Stipend?

viewpoints.name: Dr Halina Wojcik, charity director
viewpoints.text: We pay a modest stipend to twelve long-term volunteers and I will not pretend it was principled. We did it because we were losing exactly the people who could least afford to keep giving us fifteen hours a week, and the alternative to a stipend was not unpaid volunteering — it was them leaving. Retention in that group went from poor to stable. I do not claim it made anyone more committed; the ones who stayed were already the most committed, which is precisely why losing them hurt.

viewpoints.name: Callum Fitzgerald, long-serving volunteer
viewpoints.text: I have given Tuesdays to the same organisation for nine years and I would refuse a stipend. Not because I disapprove of others taking one — I would defend that. It is that the moment money enters, the relationship acquires an expectation I did not sign up for, and I would start weighing my hours against what they were worth. Right now they are worth nothing and that is the point. Offer it and let people decline; do not make it standard.

viewpoints.name: Beatriz Almeida, employment lawyer
viewpoints.text: My concern is neither moral nor budgetary, it is that organisations do this without understanding what they are creating. Regular payment for defined hours can, depending on the arrangement, look like employment — with the obligations that carry, including minimum wage, insurance and dismissal protections. Charities that stumble into that discover it during a dispute, which is the worst possible moment. Pay a stipend if you wish; take advice on the structure first, because good intentions are not a defence.

viewpoints.name: Omar Al-Rashid, community organiser
viewpoints.text: The argument is usually framed as fairness to volunteers and I would frame it as access. Unpaid volunteering is a filter: it selects for people with spare time, which means retired, comfortable or supported by someone else. Every board I have sat on has been shaped by that filter and has wondered aloud why it did not represent the community. A stipend does not solve the representation problem on its own, but refusing one guarantees the filter stays exactly where it is.
